one_liner: C++20 string types and expression-template concatenation that build strings with one allocation; 1.5-5x faster than naive std::string idioms.
what_it_does: simstr adds 'string expressions' (operator+ over literals, numbers, std::string, std::string_view and its own types) plus split, replace, trim, join, case-insensitive compare and integer/double parsing on string pieces. The header-only part (include/simstr/strexpr.h) works on standard strings (unary + turns a std::string into an expression, the result can be a std::string), while the full library adds its own owning types sstring (shared, immutable, SSO) and lstring<N> (mutable, configurable inline buffer), UTF-8/16/32 conversion through simdutf and a hash map for string keys. It is not a drop-in std::string replacement; the README expects code to be rewritten in stages.
how_it_is_fast: Expression templates compute the total length of a whole concatenation once, allocate the result once and write every piece (including numbers formatted in place) directly into it, so no temporaries or reallocations occur. lstring<N> keeps results up to N characters on the stack (the find example builds its 36-character search key without touching the heap), and integer parsing and hex/decimal formatting are inline template code instead of strtol, std::to_string or std::format. There is no SIMD in strexpr.h: substring search is a char_traits::find on the first character followed by compare, the same method libstdc++ uses.
when_to_use: Hot code that builds many short strings from literals, numbers and existing strings (log lines, keys, SQL or type names): string + number + literal into std::string ran 224 ns vs 107 ns per six concatenations (Clang 22, libstdc++) and 333 vs 215 ns (MSVC 19.44).
Hex or octal number formatting inside a concatenation: 716 ns vs 137 ns against s + std::format("{:#x}") + literal (Clang), 1018 vs 120 ns (MSVC).
Temporary keys or messages that fit a fixed stack buffer: lstringa<200> took the 'find a concatenated key' row from 114 ns to 20.0 ns on Clang/Linux and 221 to 29.3 ns under MSVC.
Splitting delimited text and parsing integers without per-part copies: 275 ns to 160 ns (Clang/Linux) and 558 ns to 220 ns (MSVC, splitf).
Code that needs the same string algorithms for char, char8_t, char16_t, char32_t and wchar_t, where std::format and std::to_chars only cover char.
when_not_to_use: You want a drop-in std::string: simstr has its own string types and only partly std-compatible methods, so adoption is a rewrite.
Single integer parsing: std::from_chars is as fast or faster (MSVC 11.9 ns vs to_int 15.5 ns; GCC 15 12.1 ns vs stringa::to_int 17.1 ns).

String-keyed hash maps on Linux: hashStrMapA (built on std::unordered_map) took 3.73 ms vs 3.64 ms for std::unordered_map<std::string> with Clang and 3.84 vs 3.64 ms with GCC; it wins only under MSVC.
Long-haystack substring search: ssa::find ties std::string_view::find on Linux (7.82 vs 7.40 ns, Clang); a SIMD searcher is the tool there.
Toolchains older than C++20, or builds that cannot take simdutf as a dependency (needed by the full library, not by strexpr.h).

integration.form: header-only (strexpr.h part) or static lib (full library: three headers and two sources)
integration.dependencies: none for strexpr.h; full library needs simdutf (CMake fetches v7.5.0); the benchmark also pulls Google Benchmark 1.9.4, fmt 12.1.0 and StringZilla main
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (concepts, std::format), CMake 3.20; README says it was checked on MSVC 19, Clang 19 and 21, GCC 13 and Emscripten 4.0.6
integration.platforms: any (portable C++ with no intrinsics in strexpr.h); author tests Windows, Linux and 32-bit WASM
integration.thread_safety: not documented; sstring shares buffers through an atomic reference count (relaxed ordering), other types are plain values
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: strexpr.h expressions accept and produce std::string and std::string_view, but split, parsing and replace use simstr types and the full speedups need stringa or lstring

gotchas: The std baselines are naive idioms: the find row builds its key with std::string{name} plus two concatenation temporaries, the std hash-map string_view row constructs a std::string on every lookup instead of using C++20 heterogeneous lookup, and the replace row appends to an unreserved std::string. Against the fastest std path in the same suite the gap narrows: hex 1.5x (Clang) to 2.1x (MSVC) vs std::to_chars, and short-text replace with std::string_view find_first_of + copy (166 ns) beats simstr's memorising variant (178 ns) on Clang.
The catalogue's asm-level label does not fit: the gains come from allocation avoidance and inline number conversion, not from vectorised scanning (find = first-character char_traits::find + compare).

sstring's reference count is decremented with std::memory_order_relaxed and the buffer freed on the last release, with no release/acquire ordering (SharedStringData::decr in sstring.h). That is the pattern std::shared_ptr avoids; on weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM, sharing one sstring across threads may race a reader's last accesses with another thread's free. x86's locked fetch_sub hides it. This is from reading the code; no failure has been reported.

Harness notes: the CHECK_RESULT answer checks are compiled out by default; StringZilla is fetched from its main branch and linked header-only with no -march flags, so its competitor rows (sz::string::find 98.6 ns vs std::string::find 7.17 ns on Clang) probably measure a serial fallback and say nothing about StringZilla; in the concat and hex rows the loop values of i (1 to 100000) are compile-time constants not hidden with DoNotOptimize.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings in this category (WojciechMula's AVX-512 string toys, sliceslice, the MSVC STL's vectorised std::search, Arm Optimized Routines) speed up scanning and copying bytes. Pick simstr when the time goes into building, formatting and splitting many short strings (temporaries, std::to_string, std::format), and pick a SIMD searcher when the cost is searching long buffers.
verified_claims_summary: The committed v2.0.0 Google Benchmark files (means of 4 repetitions, one Xeon E5-2682 v4, Linux rows under WSL) time each task against a plain std version. With Clang 22 and libstdc++: number concatenation 224 to 107 ns (2.1x), hex formatting 716 to 137 ns vs std::format (5.2x) but 207 to 137 ns vs std::to_chars (1.5x), concatenated-key find 114 to 51.3 ns (std::string result) or 20.0 ns (lstringa), conditional type-name build 59.3 to 23.6 ns, replace-while-copying 209 to 148 ns, and split plus parse 275 to 160 ns. MSVC 19.44, GCC 15.2, clang-cl and WASM runs show the same direction with different magnitudes; the README's 9-14x hex and 2-3x split figures overstate these files.
status_note: Actively maintained by one author (75 commits, v2.0.0 on 2026-10-04, 34 stars, one closed issue, vcpkg port orefkov-simstr). It is MIT-licensed, and strexpr.h alone can be vendored into a C++20 project without dependencies.
